subject: python
title: Dictionaries
description: Key/value lookup, safe access with get(), iteration, and dict comprehensions.

content.title: Definition
content.body: A dict maps hashable keys to values and looks a key up in roughly constant time regardless of size. Since Python 3.7 it also preserves insertion order.

content.title: Safe access
content.body: Indexing a missing key raises KeyError. get() returns a default instead, which is usually what you want when reading external data.
content.code:
user = {"name": "Anna"}

print(user["email"])          # KeyError
print(user.get("email"))       # None
print(user.get("email", "-"))  # -

content.title: Good practice
content.body: Iterate with .items() when you need both halves. Plain `for k in d` gives you the keys only, which is the most common source of confusion.

exercises.question: What happens on the last line?
exercises.explanation: Square-bracket access on a missing key raises KeyError. Use .get("age") to get None instead.

exercises.question: Complete the loop so it walks keys and values together.
exercises.code:
for key, value in scores.___():
    print(key, value)
exercises.explanation: .items() yields (key, value) tuples. .keys() and .values() each give you one half.

exercises.question: Which value cannot be used as a dictionary key?
exercises.explanation: Keys must be hashable, and hashability requires immutability. A list is mutable, so it raises TypeError: unhashable type.

exercises.question: What does this print?
exercises.explanation: A duplicated key is not an error — the later value simply wins, and the dict holds two entries.

exercises.question: In modern Python a dict remembers the order in which keys were inserted.
exercises.explanation: Ordering became an implementation detail in 3.6 and a language guarantee in 3.7.

exercises.question: Which line raises RuntimeError?
exercises.code:
1  d = {"a": 1, "b": 0}
2  for key in d:
3      if d[key] == 0:
4          del d[key]

answers.text: Line 2 — a dict cannot be iterated directly
Line 3 — comparison with 0 is not allowed
Line 4 — the dict changed size during iteration

exercises.explanation: Deleting while iterating invalidates the iterator. Iterate over list(d) or build a new dict instead.

exercises.question: Complete the comprehension that inverts a dict.
exercises.sentence: inverted = {v: k for k, v ___ d.items()}
exercises.explanation: A dict comprehension uses the same for ... in ... clause as a list one, with a key: value expression in front.

exercises.question: Method
exercises.back: Returns the existing value, or inserts the default and returns that
exercises.explanation: Handy for grouping: d.setdefault(k, []).append(v). collections.defaultdict(list) does the same thing more explicitly.

exercises.question: Which expression merges two dicts, letting the right-hand one win on conflicts?
exercises.explanation: Double-star unpacking merges into a new dict; a | b does the same from Python 3.9. Dicts do not support +.
